name: MathlibAnnex.Plucker.derivativeAverage
title: The set average of derivative generators

content.display_title: The set average of derivative generators
content.one_sentence_role: Separates the volume-scaled integrand from the normalization of its average.
content.natural_language_statement:
Let $n,N\in\mathbb N_0$ and give $E=\mathbb R^n$ and $F=\mathbb R^N$ their coordinate sup norms. Let $\lambda_n$ be the fixed coordinate Lebesgue measure on $E$. Let $p:E\to\mathbb R$ be a continuous real seminorm with specified constants $a_p,b_p>0$ such that
$$a_p\|x\|_\infty\le p(x)\le b_p\|x\|_\infty\qquad(x\in E).$$

The lower bound makes $p$ a norm. Its closed unit ball and real reference volume are
$$K_p=\{x:p(x)\le1\},\qquad v_p=\lambda_n(K_p)\in(0,\infty).$$
Here and below a finite Lebesgue measure is read as a real number when used as a scalar.

Let $\mathcal I_{n,N}$ be the finite set of increasing $n$-tuples of distinct rows from $\{1,\ldots,N\}$. The minor-coordinate space $\mathbb R^{\mathcal I_{n,N}}$ carries its sup norm. For a linear map $B:E\to F$, put $B_{ij}=(Be_j)_i$ in the standard coordinate basis. Write $\Pi_n(B)$ for its maximal-minor vector and $\mathcal V_p(B)$ for that vector scaled by $v_p$. Their coordinates and scaling are
$$\Pi_n(B)_I=\det(B_{i_a,j})_{a,j=1}^n,\qquad\mathcal V_p(B)=v_p\Pi_n(B)\quad(I=(i_1<\cdots<i_n)).$$

For any function $f:E\to F$, write $Df(x)$ for its Fréchet derivative where it exists and for the zero linear map otherwise. Write $G_{p,f}$ for its derivative-generator function and $\mathcal A_p(f)$ for the average of that function over $K_p$. The integrand and normalization are
$$G_{p,f}(x)=v_p\Pi_n(Df(x)),\qquad\mathcal A_p(f)=v_p^{-1}\int_{K_p}G_{p,f}(x)\,d\lambda_n(x).$$
The integrals use the fixed reference measure, even when distances are measured with $p$.
content.definition_explanation:
[The separate derivative-generator definition](https://github.com/r-tanaka-math/mathlib-annex/blob/437e6e46228bbb8e91211ebded349d7a30020e73/MathlibAnnex/Analysis/Normed/Plucker/Average.lean#L20-L24) fixes the entire integrand, coordinate by coordinate:
$$G_{p,f}(x)_I=v_p\det\big((Df(x)e_j)_{i_a}\big)_{a,j=1}^n.$$
The average uses the probability measure $v_p^{-1}\lambda_n|_{K_p}$, so the multiplier inside the integrand and the normalization outside it are distinct. If $G_{p,f}$ is integrable, evaluating a coordinate commutes with integration and gives
$$\begin{aligned}(\mathcal A_p(f))_I&=v_p^{-1}\int_{K_p}v_p\Pi_n(Df(x))_I\,d\lambda_n(x)\\&=\int_{K_p}\Pi_n(Df(x))_I\,d\lambda_n(x).\end{aligned}$$
content.assumptions: The source and target are finite real coordinate spaces with sup norms. The seminorm $p$ is continuous and has the stated positive lower and upper comparison constants. The measure is the original coordinate Lebesgue measure. No Lipschitz, differentiability or integrability condition on $f$ is part of this definition. The dimensions $n,N$ may be zero. When $n=0$, the unique empty minor has determinant $1$; when $N<n$, the minor-index set is empty and its function space has one element. Neither case is excluded.
content.conclusion: The result lies in $\mathbb R^{\mathcal I_{n,N}}$. Membership in a Plücker body requires additional hypotheses.
content.lean_realization_notes: Lean uses a total Bochner integral, equal to zero when the vector integrand is not integrable. This convention does not certify integrability. Its total derivative at a nondifferentiability point is zero; the empty determinant when $n=0$ is still $1$.
